name: Beowulf
info: Beowulf is an anonymous Old English epic of 3,182 alliterative lines, set in 5th- and 6th-century Scandinavia and preserved in a single manuscript of about 975–1025, one of the most important works of Old English literature.

facts.made: An anonymous author known as the "Beowulf poet"; its date of composition is disputed, from the 8th century to near the date of the manuscript, which was copied by two scribes
facts.form: An Old English poem of 3,182 alliterative lines, mostly in the Late West Saxon dialect with many other dialect forms
facts.where: The Nowell Codex, British Library, Cotton Vitellius A.XV, London
facts.known: Beowulf's fights with Grendel, Grendel's mother and the dragon; the mead hall Heorot; alliterative verse and kennings; the mix of pagan setting and Christian outlook; the fire of 1731; Tolkien's lecture of 1936

t: Beowulf survives only in the Nowell Codex, copied between about 975 and 1025; when the poem was composed, and whether it was passed down orally first, is still debated.
It tells of a Geatish hero who frees the Danish king Hrothgar's hall from Grendel and his mother and dies, fifty years later, fighting a dragon.
Damaged in the Ashburnham House fire of 1731, the manuscript was first transcribed in 1786, and the poem has since been translated hundreds of times.
dyk: The manuscript's shelfmark, Cotton Vitellius A.XV, means the 15th book from the left on the top shelf of the bookcase in Robert Cotton's library that had a bust of the Roman emperor Vitellius on top.
ev: King Hygelac's raid into Frisia, told in the poem, is recorded by Gregory of Tours
The only surviving manuscript, the Nowell Codex, is written by two scribes
Laurence Nowell, after whom the codex is named, most likely acquires it, according to Kevin Kiernan
Fire at Ashburnham House chars the manuscript's margins and destroys some readings
Grímur Jónsson Thorkelin makes the first transcriptions of the manuscript
Frederick Klaeber publishes the edition that becomes the central source for study of the poem
J. R. R. Tolkien's lecture Beowulf: The Monsters and the Critics opens modern criticism
Seamus Heaney's verse translation is published

sections.origins:
Beowulf is set in pagan Scandinavia in the 5th and 6th centuries and features mainly non-English characters. It blends fictional, legendary, mythic and historical elements. The hero is mentioned in no other Old English manuscript, but many of its figures, clans and events appear in Scandinavian sources, and the majority view appears to be that King Hrothgar and the Scyldings are based on historical people of 6th-century Scandinavia. The raid of King Hygelac into Frisia is mentioned by Gregory of Tours and can be dated to around 521.

Archaeology may confirm parts of the background. The western mound at Gamla Uppsala, where Snorri Sturluson placed the burial of Eadgils, held a powerful man buried around 575. At Lejre in Denmark, where tradition located Heorot, excavations found halls about 50 metres long built in the mid-6th century.

Some suggest the poem was first composed in the 7th century at Rendlesham in East Anglia, whose Wuffinga dynasty may have descended from the Geatish Wulfings; others link it to the courts of Alfred the Great or Cnut the Great. The poem's characters were Germanic pagans, but it was recorded by Christian Anglo-Saxons, most of whose people had converted around the 7th century.
sections.content:
Hrothgar, king of the Danes, has built the great hall Heorot, where he, his wife Wealhtheow and his warriors sing and feast. The monster Grendel, said to descend from the biblical Cain, attacks it and devours warriors as they sleep. Beowulf, a young warrior of the Geats, comes to help, fights Grendel without a weapon and tears off his arm. Grendel's mother then kills Hrothgar's advisor Æschere; Beowulf follows her to a lair under a lake and kills her with a giant's sword, whose blade melts in the monster's blood.

Beowulf becomes king of the Geats. Fifty years later a dragon, robbed of a golden cup from its hoard, ravages the land. Deserted by all his men but his young kinsman Wiglaf, Beowulf kills it and is mortally wounded; he is burned on a pyre and a barrow is raised for him by the sea.

The poem begins in medias res and begins and ends with funerals. Scholars have found different patterns in its design, from E. Carrigan's symmetries to Gale Owen-Crocker's four funerals and Tolkien's division between the young and the old hero. Its many digressions, once thought to interrupt the story, are now explained as comparisons with the main action that give it historical depth.
sections.making:
The date of composition is contested; the only certain date is that of the manuscript, between 975 and 1025. J. R. R. Tolkien held that the poem keeps too genuine a memory of Anglo-Saxon paganism to be much later than the Christianisation of England around 700, a view defended by Tom Shippey, Leonard Neidorf and Robert D. Fulk, who point to linguistic, metrical and naming evidence. Craig R. Davis suggests the 890s under Alfred, while others argue for an early 11th-century date. Where it was composed is also disputed: F. W. Moorman proposed Yorkshire and E. Talbot Donaldson West Mercia.

Whether it was passed down orally is debated. Albert Lord considered it proven that Beowulf was composed orally, but later scholars such as Ann Watts and Thomas Gardner argued that the text is too varied to be built wholly from set formulae, and John Miles Foley saw a continuum from tradition to text.

The verse is alliterative: each line has two halves linked by similar initial sounds. The poet drew on memorised formulae that fitted a half-line, and on kennings, such as calling the sea the "swan's riding" or a king a "ring-giver". It is written mainly in Late West Saxon with Mercian, Northumbrian, Anglian and Kentish forms, which suggests a long transmission.
sections.reception:
Scholars have long compared the poem with other traditions: the Icelandic Grettis saga, the story of Hrolf Kraki and Bodvar Bjarki, the international Bear's Son Tale and the Irish folktale of the Hand and the Child. Attempts to link it to Homer's Odyssey and Virgil's Aeneid have persisted. Its biblical parallels are more definite, with allusions to Genesis, Exodus and Daniel.

Early scholars such as Frederick Klaeber and W. P. Ker found the digressions troublesome. The history of modern criticism is often said to begin with Tolkien's 1936 lecture to the British Academy, Beowulf: The Monsters and the Critics, which argued that its literary value had been overlooked in favour of its history and that it is closer to elegy than to epic.

Its religion remains debated. Robert F. Yeager notes that its only biblical references are to the Old Testament, that Christ is never mentioned and that its characters are pagans. Fred C. Robinson reads it as a message to Christian readers about their own imperfections, Richard North as Danish myth in Christian form, and Ursula Schaefer as a poem readable within both pagan and Christian horizons. Others read it as a study of feuding or as a dynastic drama.
sections.survival:
The poem survives in a single manuscript in ink on parchment, the Nowell Codex, named after the 16th-century scholar Laurence Nowell; Kevin Kiernan argues that Nowell most likely acquired it through William Cecil in 1563. It was copied by two scribes, the first writing to line 1939 and regularising the spelling, the second keeping more archaic forms. The Old English poem Judith follows it in the same hand, and the transcription may have taken place at Malmesbury Abbey. The manuscript has no title.

It became part of Sir Robert Cotton's library, and is first identified by name in letters of 1700 between Humfrey Wanley and George Hickes. It passed to the Crown in 1702. In 1731 fire at Ashburnham House destroyed around a quarter of the Cotton manuscripts; Beowulf survived with charred margins and lost readings, and parts have crumbled since. Kiernan used fibre-optic and ultraviolet light to recover hidden letters for his Electronic Beowulf, first issued in 1999.

Grímur Jónsson Thorkelin made the first transcriptions in 1786; since the manuscript has crumbled further, they are prized witnesses, though their accuracy has been questioned. Klaeber's edition of 1922 became the central source for students and translators. The codex is in the British Library.
sections.legacy:
Beowulf is one of the most important and most often translated works of Old English literature. Sharon Turner translated selected verses into modern English in 1805, N. F. S. Grundtvig made the first complete verse translation, in Danish, in 1820, and nine complete English translations appeared in the 19th century, among them John Mitchell Kemble's and that of William Morris and A. J. Wyatt. By 2020 the Beowulf's Afterlives Bibliographic Database listed some 688 translations and other versions, in at least 38 languages besides English.

Modern translations include those of Edwin Morgan, Burton Raffel, Michael J. Alexander, Roy Liuzza and Seamus Heaney, whose version of 1999 was both praised and criticised. Tolkien's prose translation, edited by his son Christopher, appeared in 2014. Maria Dahvana Headley's novel The Mere Wife retold the story from the side of Grendel's mother, and her 2020 translation won the Hugo Award for Best Related Work.

The poem's digressions, with their impression of historical depth, were imitated by Tolkien in The Lord of the Rings, which embodies many other elements of the poem. It has also been adapted for stage and screen, and Gareth Hinds based a graphic novel of 2007 on Francis Barton Gummere's translation.

summary: Beowulf is an anonymous Old English epic of 3,182 alliterative lines about a Geatish hero who kills Grendel, Grendel's mother and a dragon. Its date of composition is disputed; it survives only in the Nowell Codex of about 975–1025, scorched in the fire of 1731, and since its first transcription in 1786 it has been edited, debated and translated hundreds of times.
